# **AI-Assisted Passive Network Forensic Framework for Enterprise Email Cryptographic Posture Assessment**

## **Executive Summary and Architectural Paradigm**

Electronic mail infrastructures represent a foundational pillar of global enterprise communication, inter-organizational identity federation, and automated transactional workflows1. Despite widespread deployment of Transport Layer Security (TLS), email protocols—specifically the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP), and Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3)—remain systematically vulnerable to cryptographic degradation, protocol downgrade attacks, and architectural misconfigurations1. While web communications have largely transitioned to mandatory encryption with strict transport policies, enterprise email continues to wrestle with backward-compatible legacy designs, opportunistic encryption models, and fragmented policy enforcement2.  
Conventional network security monitoring tools primarily perform packet decoding, protocol parsing, and perimeter intrusion detection1. Such systems extract protocol fields or identify signatures of known exploits, but they fail to synthesize packet-level cryptographic parameters into a holistic, quantifiable forensic assessment of cryptographic posture1. Consequently, Security Operations Centers (SOCs), Digital Forensics and Incident Response (DFIR) teams, and compliance auditors lack automated mechanisms to evaluate whether email sessions meet modern cryptographic standards, whether encrypted channels have been silently downgraded, or whether post-quantum cryptographic transitions are underway1.  
To resolve these operational and structural deficiencies, this report presents the technical design and theoretical grounding for an AI-assisted passive network forensic framework capable of analyzing captured network traffic (PCAP/PCAPNG files) containing email communications1. Operating strictly out-of-band and preserving digital evidence integrity, the framework reconstructs bidirectional TCP streams, parses plaintext-to-ciphertext transitions, inspects TLS handshakes, evaluates X.509 certificate chains, applies advanced multi-layer fingerprinting (JA4+, JA4X, Cisco Mercury), and combines deterministic cryptographic policy evaluation with explainable machine learning (XAI) models1. The resulting system automates cryptographic risk classification, isolates zero-day TLS protocol anomalies, quantifies organizational posture via mathematically formulated scoring algorithms, and outputs prioritized, legally defensible forensic intelligence across machine-readable and executive dashboards1.

## **Deconstruction of Contemporary Mail Protocol Attacks and Cryptographic Pitfalls**

Securing email communications presents cryptographic challenges absent from standard HTTPS architectures. The root of this vulnerability lies in the historical evolution of mail protocols, which initially transmitted all commands, credentials, and message bodies in cleartext2. When transport security was introduced, it was retrofitted onto existing application architectures via protocol extensions, establishing long-term architectural vulnerabilities2.

### **Opportunistic Encryption and the STARTTLS Dilemma**

In SMTP inter-server relaying, RFC 3207 defined the STARTTLS extension to negotiate TLS opportunistically over standard cleartext ports, such as port 252. Under opportunistic encryption, if a client or server encounters an error during the TLS handshake, or if STARTTLS is not advertised, the protocol defaults to transmitting messages in cleartext to preserve operational delivery2.  
Empirical measurements by Durumeric et al. revealed that while over 80% of monitored SMTP servers supported STARTTLS, only 35% configured certificates and parameters properly to support strict server authentication2. This fail-open paradigm allows an active on-path adversary to execute a STRIPTLS attack11. The attacker intercepts the server's initial response (such as 250-STARTTLS) and replaces it with whitespace padding or alternative capability strings2. Believing the remote endpoint lacks cryptographic capabilities, the sending client silently degrades to plaintext delivery, exposing message content, credentials, and sensitive headers to interception2.

### **Buffer Desynchronization, Command Injection, and Response Injection**

The transitional boundary between plaintext application commands and the TLS record layer introduces severe implementation hazards. In structured evaluations of email clients and servers using the EAST testing framework, Poddebniak et al. demonstrated that STARTTLS implementations across SMTP, IMAP, and POP3 suffer from deep protocol flaws3.  
The primary vulnerability involves command injection and response injection resulting from improper buffer pipelining3. RFC specifications dictate that when a server responds with 220 2.0.0 Ready to start TLS, any unencrypted application-layer read buffers must be purged, and all subsequent bytes must be processed strictly through the TLS engine3. However, numerous MTAs and Mail User Agents (MUAs) fail to clear their internal read caches3. An on-path attacker can inject cleartext application commands (such as MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, or IMAP authentication commands) into the same TCP segment as the STARTTLS command3. The receiving server buffers these commands in cleartext, initiates the TLS handshake, completes cryptographic key exchange, and then erroneously executes the unencrypted pre-handshake commands inside the secure session context3.  
Poddebniak et al. observed that over 320,000 publicly accessible email servers were vulnerable to command injection, permitting credential theft, mailbox tampering, and cross-protocol exploitation3.

### **Cross-Protocol Content Confusion: The ALPACA Attack**

The Application Layer Protocol Confusion \- Analyzing and Mitigating Cracks in TLS Authentication (ALPACA) attack exposes a systemic vulnerability in enterprise TLS deployments16. Because the core TLS protocol authenticates endpoints based on hostnames or IP addresses but does not cryptographically bind the underlying TCP destination port or application-layer protocol to the handshake, an adversary can redirect traffic between disparate services sharing a single wildcard or multi-domain Subject Alternative Name (SAN) certificate17.  
If an enterprise utilizes a single wildcard certificate across its HTTPS web server and its IMAP, POP3, or SMTP servers, an attacker intercepting browser traffic can redirect an HTTPS request to an IMAP or SMTP server18. The victim's browser initiates a TLS handshake with the mail server; because the mail server presents the valid wildcard certificate matching the requested domain, the TLS channel is successfully established17.  
Once established, the browser transmits HTTP request headers containing authentication cookies18. The mail server interprets these HTTP requests as invalid SMTP or IMAP commands, but depending on the MTA's error handling and reflection characteristics, it may echo back the payload or store it within mail spools, enabling upload attacks, download attacks, or reflected cross-site scripting18. To mitigate ALPACA, RFC 9325 mandates the deployment of the Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) extension and Server Name Indication (SNI) across non-HTTP services, strictly prohibiting certificate re-use across distinct protocol boundaries16.

### **Architectural Evolution: Deprecation via RFC 8314**

In response to the endemic weaknesses of opportunistic upgrade mechanisms, the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) issued RFC 8314, officially declaring cleartext transmission and opportunistic STARTTLS obsolete for message submission (MUA to Mail Submission Agent) and message retrieval (MUA to IMAP/POP3 Mail Access Agent)4.  
RFC 8314 strongly advises the industry to utilize Implicit TLS—establishing cryptographic handshakes immediately upon TCP connection establishment on dedicated ports—specifically port 465 for SMTP Submission (SMTPS), port 993 for IMAP over TLS (IMAPS), and port 995 for POP3 over TLS (POP3S)4. The proposed forensic framework explicitly categorizes submission or retrieval traffic utilizing opportunistic STARTTLS on legacy ports (587, 143, 110\) as an elevated security risk, rewarding infrastructures that have fully implemented implicit TLS architectures1.

## **Comparative Evaluation of Existing Network Analysis Tools and Methodologies**

Existing passive inspection solutions operate across varying layers of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) stack, yet each presents architectural limitations when evaluated against the requirements of end-to-end cryptographic forensics for mail protocols.  
Packet analyzers such as Wireshark and its headless counterpart TShark offer comprehensive protocol dissectors for TCP reassembly, SMTP command tracking, and TLS record parsing1. However, Wireshark operates as a stateless or micro-state packet inspector; it does not aggregate cryptographic metadata across historical sessions, compute multi-factor security scores, or detect subtle application-layer protocol confusion1.  
Network security monitoring platforms, most notably Zeek (formerly Bro), incorporate specialized protocol analyzers capable of tracking connection state across connection, TLS, X.509, and SMTP event logs21. Zeek natively detects when an SMTP session issues a STARTTLS command and transitions to TLS23. Furthermore, Zeek scripts validate certificate chains against local trust stores using certificate validation mechanisms comparable to modern web browsers24. Despite these capabilities, Zeek displays notable operational blind spots:

> * **Missing Intermediate Handling:** Zeek frequently raises false-positive alerts when servers fail to send intermediate certificates during the handshake, as it lacks a passive Authority Information Access (AIA) chasing cache24.  
> * **Disjointed Contextual Correlation:** Zeek logs cryptographic events across decoupled flat files, requiring complex SIEM joins or external Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents to correlate an application-layer command failure with a subsequent TLS record anomaly22.  
> * **Absence of Downgrade Causality Engines:** Zeek observes that an SMTP connection completed in plaintext, but it does not analyze whether the server's initial capabilities advertised 250-STARTTLS and were maliciously stripped in transit by an on-path adversary2.

Flow and telemetry analyzers such as Cisco Joy and Cisco Mercury advanced the domain of encrypted network traffic inspection by utilizing TLS ClientHello fingerprinting and process attribution5. Cisco Joy extracts fine-grained cryptographic features to model application behavior. Cisco Mercury extends this paradigm by fusing ClientHello parameters with network context—specifically destination IP addresses, TCP destination ports, and Server Name Indication (SNI) strings—to drive a Naive Bayes classifier that attributes encrypted flows to specific software packages or malware variants with high fidelity5. Nevertheless, Cisco Mercury is tailored primarily toward process identification and malware traffic detection; it does not audit X.509 certificate revocation status, assess forward secrecy across custom enterprise policies, evaluate mail-specific downgrade mechanisms, or score enterprise cryptographic compliance5.  
Active vulnerability scanners (such as testssl.sh or Qualys SSL Labs) provide exhaustive cryptographic configuration auditing, but they require active bidirectional probe generation, which generates intrusive network traffic, risks service disruptions on legacy embedded mail systems, and cannot evaluate past communication sessions preserved in PCAP repositories1. The proposed framework provides an out-of-band, passive counterpart that derives equivalent depth of posture assessment directly from evidentiary packet captures without transmitting a single packet1.

## **Advanced Fingerprinting and Contextual Telemetry Fusion**

Passive network analysis cannot decrypt application payloads without access to private keys or ephemeral session secrets5. Therefore, forensic attribution relies heavily on metadata modeling and cryptographic fingerprinting5. While earlier fingerprinting methods such as JA3 and JA3S provided a baseline for client-server profiling, modern network environments require the resilience of the FoxIO JA4+ suite and contextual fusion engines7.

### **Evolution Beyond JA3/JA3S Fragility**

The classical JA3 fingerprinting standard operates by computing an MD5 hash across five ClientHello fields: TLS Version, Accepted Ciphers, List of Extensions, Elliptic Curves, and Elliptic Curve Point Formats. However, JA3 exhibits severe structural fragility in modern operational environments:

> * **GREASE Pollution:** RFC 8701 introduced Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility (GREASE), wherein modern browsers and TLS stacks inject pseudo-random cipher and extension identifiers into handshakes to prevent protocol ossification. JA3 includes these randomized values in its hash, causing a single software client to produce dozens of distinct JA3 signatures7.  
> * **Cipher and Extension Ordering:** Subtle rearrangements of offered ciphers—often introduced by dynamic operating system updates or proxy intermediaries—alter the JA3 MD5 digest completely7.  
> * **Absence of Signature Algorithm Visibility:** JA3 omits the signature\_algorithms extension, blindfolding analysts to client-side signature capabilities7.

The JA4 fingerprint rectifies these limitations by implementing a structured, human- and machine-readable format structured as a\_b\_c7. Section a provides a 10-character string encoding protocol transport (t for TCP, q for QUIC), negotiated TLS version (e.g., 13 for TLS 1.3), presence of SNI (d for domain, i for IP or absent), count of offered ciphers (capped at 99), count of extensions, and the first two characters of the offered ALPN token (e.g., 00 for none, h2, or sm for SMTP)7. All GREASE values are stripped before calculating counts7. Section b consists of a 12-character truncated SHA-256 hash of the offered cipher suite identifiers, sorted in alphanumeric order to eliminate ordering artifacts7. Section c provides a 12-character truncated SHA-256 hash of sorted extension codes (omitting SNI and ALPN, which are captured in section a), followed by the list of offered signature algorithms preserved in their original advertised order7.  
By complementing JA4 with JA4S (ServerHello response fingerprinting), the forensic engine establishes high-fidelity pairings that can fingerprint specific MTA implementations (such as Postfix, Sendmail, and Microsoft Exchange Server) and isolate anomalous client connections7.

### **Certificate Attribution via JA4X**

When analyzing passive captures of TLS 1.2 sessions or cleartext certificate distribution channels, the framework extracts X.509 certificate metadata and generates JA4X fingerprints6. The JA4X algorithm constructs three distinct truncated SHA-256 hashes concatenated by underscores, representing:

> 1. The ordered Relative Distinguished Names (RDNs) of the Certificate Issuer32.  
> 2. The ordered RDNs of the Certificate Subject32.  
> 3. The structural sequence of X.509 extensions and Object Identifiers (OIDs) present within the certificate27.

JA4X abstracts away ephemeral certificate details, such as rotating serial numbers or shifting timestamps, to capture the cryptographic structure and issuance methodology of the certificate itself30. This enables the framework to attribute rogue self-signed certificates, match enterprise internal CAs, and detect infrastructure associated with command-and-control (C2) frameworks (such as Sliver or Havoc) or malicious proxy tooling deployed within the enterprise network perimeter30.

| Fingerprint Method | Scope and Input Data | Normalization Strategy | Output Structure | Primary Forensic Utility |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **JA4** | TLS ClientHello metadata7 | Strips GREASE; sorts ciphers & extensions; preserves sigalgs7 | a\_b\_c (10 chars \+ 12 hex \+ 12 hex)31 | Client software and TLS stack identification7 |
| **JA4S** | TLS ServerHello metadata7 | Strips GREASE; hashes version, cipher, and extensions7 | a\_b\_c formatted server response30 | Server MTA implementation and policy profiling7 |
| **JA4X** | X.509 Digital Certificates32 | Normalizes and hashes Issuer RDNs, Subject RDNs, and OID sequences27 | hash1\_hash2\_hash3 (3 truncated hashes)32 | Certificate lineage, C2 detection, and PKI clustering30 |
| **JA4T** | TCP SYN/SYN-ACK packet headers33 | Captures Window Size, TCP Options list, MSS, and Scale31 | window\_options\_mss\_scale string33 | Client OS kernel profiling and proxy contradiction detection34 |

### **Multi-Layer Telemetry Fusion: Integrating JA4T and Cisco Mercury Mechanics**

To detect evasion techniques—such as an attacker tool masquerading as Microsoft Outlook by spoofing ClientHello cipher arrays—the framework fuses TLS fingerprints with lower-layer transport signatures7. The system leverages JA4T to inspect the initial TCP SYN packet parameters, including TCP Window Size, Maximum Segment Size (MSS), Time-to-Live (TTL), and ordered TCP options, thereby fingerprinting the client's underlying operating system kernel33.  
A cross-layer contradiction engine correlates the TCP fingerprint against the TLS profile. A mismatch, such as a ClientHello claiming Windows 11 Outlook execution coupled with a Linux kernel TCP option sequence, triggers an automated anomaly alert, exposing synthetic traffic generation or unauthorized proxy tunneling30.  
Simultaneously, the framework incorporates Cisco Mercury’s probabilistic attribution framework by correlating the client’s offered cipher distribution with destination IP addresses, destination ports, and SNI domains5. By cross-referencing these parameters against an updated prevalence database, the engine computes a statistically sound attribution confidence score for each observed session5.

## **Passive Auditing of Modern Email Security and Routing Standards**

A complete cryptographic assessment cannot examine TLS in isolation from the identity routing structures that govern email transmission2. The forensic framework incorporates passive verification engines for Mail Transfer Agent Strict Transport Security (MTA-STS) and DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE)12.

### **Passive Auditing of MTA-STS (RFC 8461\)**

MTA-STS enables receiving domains to mandate TLS encryption for inbound SMTP connections by publishing a cryptographic policy via HTTPS and signaling its existence through DNS36. The protocol operates via two interlocking records: a DNS TXT record published at \_mta-sts.\<domain\> containing a version string and policy ID tag, and a static policy file hosted at https://mta-sts.\<domain\>/.well-known/mta-json.txt defining the operational mode (enforce, testing, or none), maximum age, and allowable MX hostnames36.  
In a purely passive inspection posture, the framework inspects captured DNS transactions within the PCAP22. When outbound SMTP connections are observed to an MX destination, the engine searches prior or concurrent DNS responses for the corresponding \_mta-sts TXT record12. When an active policy is identified, the framework verifies that the subsequent SMTP session initiated STARTTLS and that the presented server certificate matches one of the MX patterns designated in the policy36.  
If an SMTP connection to a known MTA-STS-enforcing domain occurs entirely in cleartext without a corresponding \_mta-sts DNS query, or if the DNS response returned an NXDOMAIN or empty response while enterprise threat intelligence indicates an active policy exists, the engine flags an active MTA-STS Downgrade or DNS Suppression Attack37.

### **Passive Auditing of DANE for SMTP (RFC 7672\)**

DANE leverages the DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) hierarchy to bind TLS server certificates or public keys directly to the domain name via DNS TLSA resource records12. This eliminates reliance on centralized public Certificate Authorities (CAs) and blocks on-path certificate substitution12.  
The passive forensic framework extracts captured DNS responses containing TLSA records matching the port 25 pattern (\_25.\_tcp.mx1.example.com)38. When a TLSA record is detected, the engine decodes its four constituent parameters: Certificate Usage, Selector, Matching Type, and Certificate Association Data38. The engine parses the certificate presented by the server during the subsequent TLS handshake, computes the corresponding cryptographic hash across the certificate or its public key according to the TLSA selector and matching-type rules, and compares the result against the captured TLSA record1. Any mismatch immediately indicates active tampering, DNS cache poisoning, or catastrophic certificate rotation failure35.

| Standard / Protocol | RFC Reference | Policy Discovery Mechanism | Primary Attack Mitigated | Passive Forensic Audit Indicator |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **MTA-STS** | RFC 846137 | DNS TXT (\_mta-sts) \+ HTTPS JSON policy36 | STARTTLS stripping, on-path MitM36 | Missing TLS upgrade despite published STS record; invalid MX matching36 |
| **DANE for SMTP** | RFC 767212 | DNSSEC-validated DNS TLSA records35 | Rogue CA issuance, on-path cert substitution12 | Discrepancy between presented TLS cert and parsed TLSA record hash1 |

| **TLS Hardening** | RFC 932520 | In-band TLS Handshake extensions20 | Protocol downgrade, cross-protocol attacks (ALPACA)18 | Negotiation of TLS \< 1.2; missing ALPN/SNI on shared certificates18 |

## **Post-Quantum Cryptographic Readiness and Cryptographic Drift Tracking**

As cryptographic architectures evolve toward quantum-resistant algorithms to combat the "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" (HNDL) paradigm—wherein adversaries record encrypted enterprise communications today to decrypt them once cryptographically relevant quantum computers emerge—monitoring post-quantum readiness has become an operational necessity29.

### **Passive Visibility into TLS 1.3 Post-Quantum Key Exchange**

The transition to post-quantum cryptography in TLS 1.3 centers on hybrid key exchange mechanisms, combining classical elliptic curves (such as X25519) with lattice-based key encapsulation mechanisms standardized by NIST (FIPS 203 ML-KEM)42.  
The forensic framework evaluates post-quantum readiness passively by inspecting unencrypted fields within the TLS 1.3 ClientHello and ServerHello handshake messages6. Handshake inspection focuses on two key extensions:

> * **Supported Groups Extension (0x000a):** The client advertises supported key exchange groups29. The framework tracks specific post-quantum and hybrid named group codepoints, most notably X25519MLKEM768 (codepoint 0x11ec), as well as interim draft or experimental identifiers (0xfe31, 0x6399)28.  
> * **Key Share Extension (0x0033):** The engine analyzes the client's offered key shares and the server's selected key share29. While a classical X25519 key share requires 32 bytes of public key data, a hybrid X25519MLKEM768 key share transmits a 1,216-byte payload (combining the 32-byte X25519 key with the 1,184-byte ML-KEM-768 public key)44.

| PQC State Identifier | Classification State | Handshake Observation Criteria | Cryptographic Risk Evaluation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **State 0** | Legacy Classical | Handshake offers and negotiates solely classical groups (e.g., secp256r1, x25519)29 | Critical exposure to retrospective Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks41 |
| **State 1** | PQC Offered, Classical Selected | Client advertises 0x11ec in supported\_groups, but ServerHello selects classical group29 | Endpoint capability gap; server infrastructure lacks PQC implementation6 |
| **State 2** | Hybrid PQC Negotiated | Server selects 0x11ec (X25519MLKEM768) in key\_share extension44 | Hardened posture; quantum-resistant confidentiality established29 |
| **State 3** | Pure Post-Quantum | Key exchange established via non-hybrid quantum-safe KEM (future profiles)29 | Maximum quantum resistance; compliance with advanced post-quantum mandates29 |

### **Protocol Fragmentation and Longitudinal Drift Tracking**

The introduction of large post-quantum public keys and certificates expands the size of the initial ClientHello and subsequent handshake records beyond standard network Maximum Transmission Units (MTUs, typically 1,500 bytes)44. Consequently, handshakes are frequently fragmented across multiple TCP segments44. Passive frameworks parsing packets on an isolated, datagram-by-datagram basis fail to recognize the fragmented TLS records. The proposed framework resolves this via an in-memory, zero-copy TCP stream reassembly engine that buffers out-of-order segments and completely reassembles the record layer before dispatching the payload to the cryptographic parser1.  
Furthermore, enterprise infrastructures undergo continuous modification, including software patches, certificate rotations, and cipher renegotiations6. The framework implements longitudinal baseline tracking by maintaining historical records of cryptographic profiles per server 5-tuple and fully qualified domain name (FQDN)6. When analyzing PCAP captures spanning multiple temporal windows, the drift engine detects regressions:

> * Cipher suite degradation, such as a server historically negotiating TLS\_AES\_256\_GCM\_SHA384 suddenly reverting to CBC-mode ciphers1.  
> * Key length regression, where a certificate renewal inadvertently reduces an RSA public key size from 4096 bits to 1024 or 2048 bits1.  
> * STARTTLS feature disappearance, where an MTA that previously enforced encryption ceases advertising STARTTLS in response to EHLO queries2.  
> * Post-quantum drift, where sessions regress from hybrid post-quantum key establishment back to classical parameters due to upstream middlebox interference6.

## **Hybrid Machine Learning, Risk Scoring, and Explainable AI Architecture**

To ensure operational utility within enterprise SOC and DFIR workflows, network forensic tools must minimize false alarms while delivering transparent, auditable conclusions1. Relying solely on deep neural networks or opaque machine learning models introduces unacceptable legal and forensic risks, as black-box classifiers cannot produce the deterministic evidence required during security audits or regulatory breach investigations1. The proposed framework overcomes this by implementing a dual-engine architecture: a deterministic Cryptographic Policy Engine coupled with an Explainable Machine Learning (XAI) Analytics Engine1.

### **Deterministic Cryptographic Rule Engine**

The deterministic engine evaluates reconstructed handshakes and certificates against absolute cryptographic standards, including NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, BSI TR-02102-2, RFC 8996, and RFC 93251. This engine issues immediate forensic violations across non-negotiable failure states:

> * Use of deprecated protocols, including SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.11.  
> * Insecure symmetric ciphers, including NULL ciphers, export-grade ciphers, RC4, 3DES, static DES, and IDEA1.  
> * Unauthenticated or non-forward-secret key exchanges, including static RSA, static Diffie-Hellman, and anonymous DH (ADH)1.  
> * Broken hash algorithms in digital signatures, such as MD5 and SHA-11.  
> * X.509 certificate anomalies, including expired validity dates, self-signed certificates in public contexts, mismatched SAN hostnames, and insufficient key lengths (RSA \< 2048 bits, ECC \< 256 bits)1.  
> * Active protocol downgrade or command injection indicators3.

### **Supervised Classification via Cost-Sensitive Random Forest**

For multi-class risk classification into LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL tiers, the framework deploys a supervised Random Forest classifier trained on tabular security vectors1. Random Forest models provide high resilience against feature multi-collinearity, handle mixed categorical and continuous data cleanly without distorting scale, and exhibit minimal susceptibility to overfitting when tuned with appropriate tree-depth constraints1.

### **Unsupervised TLS Anomaly Detection via Isolation Forest**

Novel attack variants, custom tunneling mechanisms, and zero-day protocol smuggling frequently bypass deterministic policy rules1. To isolate such sessions, the framework integrates an unsupervised Isolation Forest model1.  
Isolation Forest isolates anomalous observations by randomly selecting a feature and randomly selecting a split value between the maximum and minimum values of that feature1. Because anomalies inherently exhibit distinct attribute configurations (such as non-standard extension sequences, abnormal byte proportions prior to handshake, or rare cipher-curve combinations), they require significantly fewer recursive splits to be isolated in isolation trees1.  
The anomaly score ![][image7] for an instance ![][image8] across an ensemble of ![][image9] trees is computed as: $$s(x, n) \= 2^{-\\frac{\\mathbb{E}(h(x))}{c(n)}}$$where ![][image10] is the path length to isolate instance ![][image8], ![][image11] is the average path length across all trees, and ![][image12] is the average path length of unsuccessful searches in a Binary Search Tree:

Instances yielding an anomaly score ![][image14] are marked as suspicious and routed for forensic deep-dive analysis1.

| **Forward Secrecy (![][image29])** | 0.10 | Hybrid PQC \= 100; ECDHE \= 90; DHE \= 70; Static RSA \= 01 | Absence of Forward Secrecy: ![][image25] \[cite: 1\] |
| **Protocol Context (![][image30])** | 0.10 | SMTPS/IMAPS/POP3S \= 100; Port 587 Submission \= 80; Cleartext Port 25 \= 201 | ALPACA Protocol Confusion Vulnerability: ![][image25] \[cite: 18\] |

The composite Enterprise Posture Index is computed across the dataset as the volume-weighted harmonic mean of session scores, penalizing environments with long tails of degraded legacy sessions:  
![][image31]  
where ![][image32] represents the data volume or packet count of session ![][image33]. Final posture bands are categorized into standardized operational tiers:

> * **90 – 100 (Excellent):** Hardened cryptographic environment enforcing TLS 1.3 or Implicit TLS with active hybrid post-quantum key establishment1.  
> * **75 – 89 (Good):** Fully compliant posture negotiating TLS 1.2 or modern TLS 1.3 with forward secrecy, exhibiting minor non-critical configuration deprecations1.  
> * **50 – 74 (Moderate):** Elevated risk posture where legacy CBC cipher suites or opportunistic STARTTLS negotiations are prevalent1.  
> * **25 – 49 (Poor):** Severe organizational exposure characterized by deprecated TLS 1.0 or 1.1 sessions, expired certificates, or non-forward-secret key exchanges1.  
> * **0 – 24 (Critical):** Active compromise indicators, including detected STARTTLS stripping, command injection, cleartext credential transmissions, or export-grade ciphers1.

### **Model Explainability via TreeSHAP**

To eliminate the operational opacity of machine learning decisions, the framework embeds TreeSHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations for tree-based models)46. For any session classified as HIGH or CRITICAL risk, the system extracts the exact local Shapley feature attributions:  
![][image34]  
where ![][image35] is the base expected model output across the training distribution, and ![][image36] represents the exact marginal contribution of feature ![][image6] toward pushing the risk prediction away from the baseline48. When an incident responder examines an alert, the interface renders quantitative feature attributions rather than an opaque risk label, explaining the exact mathematical influence of stripped upgrades, weak ciphers, or certificate validation flaws46.

## **End-to-End System Pipeline and Operational Deliverables**

The forensic framework processes captured packet evidence through eight tightly coupled architectural layers, guaranteeing chain-of-custody preservation and evidentiary reproducibility1.

### **Comprehensive Processing Architecture**

> 1. **Evidence Ingestion and Hash Integrity:** The processing pipeline accepts raw PCAP and PCAPNG capture files, computing cryptographic integrity hashes (SHA-256 and HMAC) across the container to preserve evidentiary integrity prior to dissection1. Memory-mapped zero-copy packet buffering streams headers directly into memory, preventing host memory exhaustion during multi-gigabyte captures1.  
> 2. **Stream Reassembly and Protocol Demultiplexing:** The TCP stream engine reassembles bidirectional segments across the TCP 5-tuple, resolving packet retransmissions and out-of-order arrivals1. Protocol demultiplexing occurs dynamically via deep application-layer signatures (such as regex matching of SMTP EHLO/HELO, IMAP CAPABILITY, and POP3 STLS banners) rather than relying on static port allocations1.  
> 3. **Application Upgrade and Transition Analysis:** A dedicated state machine tracks application commands through four upgrade phases: capability advertising, upgrade request, server acknowledgment, and TLS record layer initiation1. The engine identifies silent fallbacks to cleartext and checks TCP segment boundaries for buffer pipelining anomalies characteristic of command and response injection attacks1.  
> 4. **TLS Dissection and Cryptographic Parsing:** Reconstructed TLS handshakes are parsed to extract offered and negotiated protocol versions, cipher suites, elliptic curve groups, supported signature algorithms, and TLS extensions (such as SNI, ALPN, Supported Groups, and Key Share)1. Forward secrecy is explicitly audited based on whether key exchange relies on ephemeral mechanisms1.  
> 5. **X.509 Certificate Path Validation:** Leaf and intermediate certificates are parsed from handshakes to extract Subject, Issuer, Serial Numbers, validity windows, and Subject Alternative Names1. The engine audits public key algorithms, verifies bit lengths against policy minimums, checks signature hashing algorithms, and validates certificate paths against embedded enterprise trust stores1.  
> 6. **Multi-Layer Fingerprinting:** Handshake parameters generate JA4 client and JA4S server fingerprints, while certificate structures produce JA4X hashes7. TCP SYN packets are processed to extract JA4T network stack fingerprints, feeding the cross-layer contradiction engine to identify client spoofing33.  
> 7. **Compliance Audit, Anomaly Detection, and Posture Scoring:** The deterministic rule engine evaluates handshakes against international compliance standards, while the cost-sensitive Random Forest and Isolation Forest models generate risk classifications and anomaly scores1. The session posture score (![][image37]) is calculated alongside TreeSHAP feature attributions1.  
> 8. **Forensic Deliverable Generation:** Final outputs are serialized into machine-readable JSON formats, structured Cryptographic Software Bills of Materials (CycloneDX CBOM), auditable PDF reports, and an interactive monitoring dashboard1.

### **Forensic Data Schema and Exportable Artifacts**

The framework serializes analysis outputs into a comprehensive JSON format designed for SIEM and SOAR ingestion, structured to provide complete forensic traceability1.

| JSON Schema Section | Constituent Fields | Forensic Relevance |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| forensic\_metadata | pcap\_file, sha256\_hash, analyst\_id, timestamp\_utc | Guarantees chain of custody and forensic reproducibility1 |
| session\_summary | session\_id, flow\_5tuple, protocol, channel\_architecture, posture\_score, risk\_tier | High-level session indexing and multi-factor posture metrics1 |
| cryptographic\_analysis | starttls\_state, tls\_version, cipher\_suite, forward\_secrecy, pqc\_status, cmd\_inject | Low-level cryptographic and transition parameters1 |
| fingerprints | ja4, ja4s, ja4x, ja4t, cisco\_mercury\_attribution | Multi-layer client, server, OS, and certificate lineage tracking5 |
| findings | Array of finding\_id, severity, type, description, evidence\_packet\_indices | Detailed vulnerability findings tied directly to packet offsets1 |
| explainability | model\_version, base\_value, shap\_feature\_attributions | Transparent Shapley mathematical weightings justifying risk score46 |
| mitigations | Array of actionable technical remediation steps | Contextual guidance for network and mail systems administrators1 |

### **Interactive Visualization Dashboard Architecture**

The web-based visualization interface translates dense forensic metadata into actionable operational intelligence across four specialized views1:

> * **Executive Posture Console:** Features enterprise score dial indicators, longitudinal posture drift timelines, and protocol distributions across SMTP, IMAP, and POP31.  
> * **Session Forensic Inspector:** Provides a synchronized multi-pane timeline displaying reconstructed application commands, TCP segment alignment, binary TLS record decodes, and parsed X.509 certificate chains1.  
> * **Explainability and Attribution Explorer:** Renders interactive TreeSHAP waterfall charts for high-risk sessions, illustrating how specific parameters (such as stripped STARTTLS or weak 3DES ciphers) drove the risk classification1.  
> * **Post-Quantum Readiness Matrix:** Visualizes the proportion of enterprise mail sessions utilizing hybrid quantum-safe key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) versus classical groups across internal and external subnets29.

## **Novel Architectural Contributions and Technical Differentials**

The proposed forensic framework advances beyond traditional network analysis tools through four core innovations:

### **1\. STARTTLS Downgrade Causality Graph Engine**

Existing tools merely observe whether TLS was established on an observed connection1. The proposed solution introduces an automated causality engine that models the entire application upgrade sequence as a directed state machine1. By computing the delta between advertised server capabilities (250-STARTTLS) and subsequent client commands within the same TCP stream, the engine isolates active on-path stripping attacks from passive configuration oversights2. Furthermore, by monitoring TCP segment boundaries during the upgrade phase, the causality engine detects pre-handshake buffer pipelining, actively identifying command and response injection vulnerabilities before malicious payloads compromise application spools3.

### **2\. Multi-Layer Telemetry and Infrastructure Correlation**

Rather than relying on isolated fingerprint hashes such as JA3, the framework unifies client TLS fingerprinting (JA4), server response profiling (JA4S), certificate structural hashing (JA4X), TCP network stack profiling (JA4T), and contextual IP and SNI fusion (Cisco Mercury)5. This multi-layer approach exposes client emulation attacks (such as malicious bots spoofing Outlook TLS parameters while exhibiting Linux kernel TCP options) and clusters rogue internal mail servers or C2 frameworks sharing certificate generation templates30.

### **3\. Integrated Post-Quantum Cryptographic Readiness and Drift Auditing**

Existing enterprise tools lack visibility into post-quantum migration dynamics41. The proposed framework natively decodes TLS 1.3 supported\_groups and key\_share extensions to classify sessions into four discrete PQC states29. By tracking hybrid X25519MLKEM768 adoptions alongside classical algorithms across temporal capture baselines, the platform operates as an automated Cryptographic Software Bill of Materials (CBOM) generator and cryptographic drift monitor, alerting organizations to unintended cryptographic regressions or middlebox-induced fallbacks6.

### **4\. Hybrid Deterministic Policy Coupled with Explainable AI**

Pure machine learning models are inherently unsuited for regulatory digital forensics due to their black-box nature and susceptibility to hallucinations1. Conversely, purely static rule engines fail to catch emerging anomalies1. This framework resolves the dilemma through a hybrid architecture: it enforces deterministic compliance checks based on international standards (NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, RFC 8314, RFC 9325\) for legally defensible reporting, while deploying Cost-Sensitive Random Forest and Isolation Forest models to isolate zero-day protocol anomalies, with every machine learning decision explained via TreeSHAP feature attribution1.

## **Implementation Roadmap**

To transition the proposed architecture into a production-grade enterprise forensic framework, engineering execution is structured across four distinct phases spanning a 24-week development cycle1.

| Phase | Milestone Name | Duration | Key Technical Deliverables | Validation Criteria |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Phase 1** | Core Ingestion & Stream Reassembly | Weeks 1–6 | Zero-copy PCAP ingestion, bidirectional TCP reassembly, application demuxing for SMTP/IMAP/POP31. | Zero packet drop on 10 Gbps PCAP replay; 100% protocol demux accuracy on standard test corpus1. |
| **Phase 2** | Cryptographic & Upgrade Dissection | Weeks 7–12 | STARTTLS state machine, buffer desync detection, TLS 1.2/1.3 parsing, X.509 validation, JA4+/JA4X/JA4T fingerprinting1. | Accurate identification of synthetic EAST command injection and STARTTLS stripping test PCAPs3. |
| **Phase 3** | Analytics, Machine Learning & XAI | Weeks 13–18 | Rule engine (NIST/RFC 8314/9325), Random Forest risk classifier, Isolation Forest anomaly model, TreeSHAP integration1. | Macro F1-score ![][image38] across risk tiers; sub-second SHAP explanation generation per alert1. |
| **Phase 4** | Dashboard, CBOM & Enterprise Reporting | Weeks 19–24 | Web console development, JSON CBOM export, automated PDF/HTML forensic report generator, temporal drift engine1. | Successful end-to-end audit of enterprise email PCAPs; verification of CycloneDX CBOM interoperability1. |

Through this phased implementation, the framework delivers an end-to-end, out-of-band analytical platform that transforms raw packet captures into an explainable, prioritized, and quantum-aware cryptographic assessment of enterprise email environments1.
